title: RBAC v2 evaluation flow scratchpad (gateway -> service) + caching ideas + library APIs
content:
Context / why this doc exists
- We need a single mental model for where/when RBAC decisions happen across: API Gateway, Control Plane services, Console backend, and (eventually) private installer/admin flows.
- Goal is consistent deny-by-default enforcement + low latency + auditability.
- This is a scratchpad for evaluation flow + caching approaches + what the shared authz library should look like.

Non-goals (for this scratchpad)
- Not a full policy language design.
- Not deciding storage schema (bindings/policy bundle versioning covered elsewhere).


0) Terminology (quick)
- subject: authenticated principal (user, service account, API key)
- action: permission string (e.g., "controlplane.routingPolicies.update")
- resource: {type, id} (optional for v2, but we should standardize shape)
- scope: org/project/environment/cluster scoping tuple used by policy evaluator
- decision: allow | deny
- reasons: structured reason codes (for debugging + audit, not always user-visible)


1) High-level evaluation options (what we’re converging on)
We have three realistic placements:
(A) gateway-only: gateway checks everything, services assume allowed
(B) service-only: services check, gateway mostly authn + routing
(C) split/hybrid: gateway enforces coarse baseline + services enforce authoritative fine-grain

Working stance (aligns with ADR-015 direction):
- Services MUST be able to enforce authorization themselves (defense-in-depth; avoids bypass via internal routing paths).
- Gateway enforces deny-by-default for external traffic and blocks obviously unauthenticated/unscoped requests early.
- We allow gateway to short-circuit ALLOW for some low-risk routes only if we can guarantee equivalence + audit consistency (tbd; likely we keep gateway as “enforce + annotate”, service as “authoritative”).


2) Request flow diagrams (text)

2.1 External request: Hosted API / Console -> Gateway -> Control Plane service

  [Client]
     |
     | 1. HTTP request (Authorization: Bearer ... / API key)
     v
  [API Gateway]
     |
     | 2. AuthN (verify token/key; map to subject)
     | 3. Derive request context (org_id, project_id, env_id if present)
     | 4. Determine action (permission) from route annotation
     | 5. AuthZ evaluate (policy evaluator client, cached)
     | 6. If deny => 403 + reason code (admin debug header optional)
     | 7. If allow => forward to service, include AuthZ context headers
     v
  [Control Plane Service]
     |
     | 8. Service-level AuthZ check (same action + scope; authoritative)
     |    - for non-external entrypoints, this is the only gate
     | 9. Execute business logic
     | 10. Emit audit log event with authz decision context
     v
  [DB / downstream]


2.2 Internal request: service -> service (no gateway)

  [Service A]
     |
     | 1. Calls Service B (mTLS / internal token)
     | 2. Propagates end-user subject context OR uses service principal
     v
  [Service B]
     |
     | 3. Service-level AuthZ check (always)
     | 4. Emit audit log if security-relevant action (even if deny)

Notes:
- We need a clear rule for whether we propagate end-user subject vs service principal (impacts least privilege + audit). Default should be end-user subject when acting on behalf of a user.


2.3 Private deployments (VPC/on-prem)
Same logical flow; differences:
- “Gateway” may be NGINX/Envoy fronting control plane, but the semantics stay.
- IdP group mapping may be different; policy bundle distribution is controlled by private control plane.


3) Canonical inputs/outputs for evaluation

3.1 Proposed evaluation request struct (language-agnostic)
- subject:
  - type: user | service_account | api_key | internal_service
  - id: stable UUID
  - org_id: required
  - session_id: optional (useful for audit trace)
  - authn_method: oidc | saml | api_key | mTLS
- action: string (permission)
- scope:
  - org_id: required
  - project_id: optional
  - env_id: optional
  - cluster_id: optional (Dedicated/Private)
- resource (optional v2, but we should reserve field):
  - type: e.g. routing_policy, api_key, audit_log_export
  - id: string
- context:
  - request_id / trace_id
  - deployment_mode: hosted | dedicated | private
  - region

3.2 Proposed evaluation response
- decision: ALLOW | DENY
- reason_code: enum (e.g., SUBJECT_MISSING_SCOPE, PERMISSION_NOT_GRANTED, POLICY_VERSION_MISMATCH, BINDING_NOT_FOUND)
- reason_detail: string (safe summary; do not include secrets)
- policy_version: string (bundle version/hash)
- cache:
  - cache_hit: bool
  - ttl_remaining_ms: int


4) Caching ideas (safe-by-default)

4.1 Core principle
Cache ALLOW decisions carefully; DENY decisions are safer to cache short-term but risk masking newly granted access (UX issue) rather than security issue.

4.2 Cache key
cache_key = hash(subject_id, subject_type, org_id, action, scope_tuple, policy_version?)

Important: include scope dimensions explicitly.
- If request is org-scoped only: scope_tuple = (org_id)
- If project/env present: scope_tuple = (org_id, project_id, env_id)
- If cluster present: (org_id, cluster_id) or (org_id, project_id, cluster_id) depending on semantics


4.3 What to include re: policy version
Two patterns:
Pattern 1: policy_version in cache key
- Pro: safe invalidation when roles/bindings update and policy version changes
- Con: requires reliable versioning signal available at evaluation point

Pattern 2: cache stores {decision, policy_version} and we validate against current version
- Pro: smaller keyspace
- Con: requires cheap “current version” lookup

Working direction (consistent w/ our PR prototypes):
- Use policy_version in key where available; fall back to short TTL + invalidation hooks.


4.4 TTL guidance (starting point, needs perf testing)
- ALLOW: 30s default TTL
- DENY: 5s default TTL
- Hard cap: 5m (we should not exceed this unless we have strong invalidation)

Rationale:
- Role binding changes are relatively rare but high-impact; shorter TTL reduces risk of stale allows.
- We can compensate with invalidation triggers on writes.


4.5 Invalidation triggers (best-effort + defense-in-depth)
On any mutation to roles/permissions/bindings:
- increment org_authz_epoch (monotonic int) OR rotate policy_version
- publish invalidation event:
  - {org_id, project_id?, env_id?, subject_id?, epoch}
Consumers:
- gateway authz cache
- service authz cache

Notes:
- For Private: invalidation event mechanism might be local (Redis pubsub / in-memory fanout) instead of global.
- If invalidation fails, TTL acts as fallback.


4.6 Caching placement
Option A: only gateway caches
Option B: each service caches
Option C: shared sidecar cache

Likely path:
- Gateway caches (biggest win, highest traffic)
- Services cache locally (for internal calls + defense-in-depth). Keep service cache size bounded.


4.7 Failure modes & required behavior
- Policy evaluator timeout:
  - default: FAIL CLOSED (deny) for sensitive actions
  - we may allow explicit “fail-open” ONLY for low-risk read-only routes and only with explicit approval + metrics (but avoid; SOC2/evidence wants deterministic deny-by-default)
- Cache backend unavailable:
  - evaluate without cache (if possible)
  - if evaluator also down -> deny

Observability required:
- authz_eval_latency_ms
- authz_cache_hit_rate
- authz_denies_total{action, reason_code}
- authz_evaluator_errors_total


5) Proposed shared library APIs
We have two consumers: (1) gateway middleware, (2) service interceptors (gRPC/HTTP).

5.1 Go-ish interface (control plane services)

// Construct once at startup
client := authz.NewClient(authz.Config{
  EvaluatorURL: "http://policy-evaluator...",
  Cache: authz.NewInMemoryCache(authz.CacheConfig{MaxEntries: 200000, DefaultAllowTTL: 30*time.Second, DefaultDenyTTL: 5*time.Second}),
  Metrics: metrics,
  Logger: logger,
})

// In request handler
func (h *Handler) UpdateRoutingPolicy(ctx context.Context, req *UpdateRoutingPolicyRequest) (*UpdateRoutingPolicyResponse, error) {
  subj := authz.SubjectFromContext(ctx) // set by authn middleware
  scope := authz.Scope{OrgID: req.OrgId, ProjectID: req.ProjectId, EnvID: req.EnvId}

  decision, err := client.Authorize(ctx, authz.Request{
    Subject: subj,
    Action: permissions.ControlPlaneRoutingPoliciesUpdate,
    Scope: scope,
    Resource: authz.Resource{Type: "routing_policy", ID: req.PolicyId},
  })
  if err != nil { return nil, status.Error(codes.PermissionDenied, "permission denied") }
  if !decision.Allowed {
    return nil, authz.ToStatusError(decision) // attaches reason_code in metadata for admins
  }

  // business logic...
}

Key helpers we want:
- SubjectFromContext (standard)
- ToStatusError / ToHTTPError (standard error mapping)
- decision struct that carries policy_version + reason_code + safe message


5.2 TypeScript-ish interface (console backend / node services)

const client = new AuthzClient({
  evaluatorUrl: process.env.POLICY_EVAL_URL,
  cache: new LruCache({ maxEntries: 50000, allowTtlMs: 30000, denyTtlMs: 5000 }),
});

export async function requirePermission(ctx: RequestContext, action: Permission, scope: Scope, resource?: Resource) {
  const decision = await client.authorize({
    subject: ctx.subject,
    action,
    scope,
    resource,
    requestId: ctx.requestId,
  });

  if (!decision.allowed) {
    throw toHttp403(decision, { includeDebugHeader: ctx.subject.isAdmin });
  }
}


5.3 Annotations / route mapping (to avoid “stringly typed” permissions)
We need a route->permission mapping that’s validated in CI.

Gateway side:
- Each route definition must declare action (permission) + scope extraction function
- Middleware enforces: if route missing annotation => deny (or fail deployment)

Service side:
- Each handler must call requirePermission OR have an explicit @NoAuthzRequired annotation that is audited + reviewed.


6) Scope extraction (where bugs happen)

6.1 Common patterns
- org_id in path: /v1/orgs/{org_id}/...
- project_id in path: /v1/orgs/{org_id}/projects/{project_id}/...
- env_id sometimes in body (bad for gateway): /v1/.../deployments:update { env_id: ... }

Gateway scope derivation rules (proposal):
1) Prefer path params. If env_id only in body, gateway can’t cheaply parse for streaming/big bodies.
2) If body-only scope is needed:
   - either move env_id into path for new endpoints
   - or have gateway evaluate at org-scope only and require service-level check with env scope (but then gateway becomes less useful)

Action item:
- Flag endpoints with body-only scope in inventory; decide per endpoint whether to refactor path.


6.2 Multi-deployment scope additions
Dedicated/Private introduces cluster_id.
Examples:
- “restart model server on cluster” => scope must include cluster_id
- “view cluster logs” => cluster_id + maybe env_id

We need a deterministic scope hierarchy:
- org > project > env > cluster (not strictly a tree across all products; cluster might be parallel)

Open question:
- Do we allow bindings at org-level to grant permissions over all clusters? Probably yes for Org Admin.


7) Auditing: what to log at decision time
We should be consistent so auditors can answer “who could do what” and “who did what”.

For security-relevant actions, emit audit events that include:
- subject_id, subject_type
- action (permission)
- scope tuple
- resource (type/id)
- decision allow/deny
- reason_code (if deny)
- policy_version
- request_id/trace_id
- enforcement_point: gateway | service

Important: if gateway denies before request hits service, we still need an audit event.
- Option 1: gateway emits audit event directly
- Option 2: gateway emits a structured security log; later shipped to audit pipeline

Preference:
- Gateway emits an audit event for DENY and ALLOW? Probably only DENY + high-risk ALLOW to control volume.
- Services emit audit event for actual mutations (ground truth “did happen”).


8) Denial reason codes (rough list)
(Align w/ “deny reason codes standardization” thread + debug header work.)
- AUTHN_REQUIRED
- SUBJECT_NOT_IN_ORG
- SCOPE_MISSING_PROJECT
- SCOPE_MISSING_ENV
- PERMISSION_NOT_GRANTED
- ROLE_BINDING_NOT_FOUND
- POLICY_NOT_LOADED
- POLICY_EVALUATOR_TIMEOUT
- POLICY_VERSION_STALE
- BREAK_GLASS_REQUIRED (if we gate some ops behind explicit elevation)

Exposure policy:
- User-facing: generic "permission denied" + link to docs
- Admin debug: X-Redwood-Authz-Deny-Reason: <code> + Request-Id


9) Streaming endpoints / edge cases
We already saw a missing check / bypass risk on streaming routes.
Lessons:
- Middleware must run before stream is established.
- Ensure route annotations apply equally to streaming and non-streaming variants.
- Tests: must include streaming paths in critical permission E2E.


10) Performance notes / back-of-envelope
Targets:
- Gateway additional p95 latency overhead: <= 2ms when cache hit
- Cache hit rate: > 95% for steady-state interactive workloads
- Evaluator call p95: < 15ms within region

If we can’t hit this, options:
- push evaluator closer (in-process embedded library w/ local policy bundle)
- precompute subject->permission bitsets per scope (careful: scope explosion)


11) TODOs / open questions
- Decide final “authoritative enforcement point” language for docs: gateway + service both enforce, service is authoritative.
- Confirm whether gateway should emit audit events for denies (and where that pipeline lives).
- Determine exact cache key + whether to include policy_version in key (need final policy versioning semantics).
- Scope model: confirm env_id vs cluster_id precedence for Dedicated/Private ops.
- Define standard context propagation headers gateway -> service:
  - X-Redwood-Subject-Id
  - X-Redwood-Org-Id
  - X-Redwood-Authz-Policy-Version
  - X-Redwood-Request-Id
  (Need review: don’t allow spoofing; should be internal-only + stripped from external requests.)
- Inventory endpoints where scope is in body; decide refactor vs service-only enforcement.


12) Quick notes from recent discussions (paste)
- “Deny-by-default” means: if permission annotation missing OR evaluator errors => deny; exceptions require explicit allowlist + sign-off.
- Break-glass: should be modeled as a time-bound role binding; evaluator doesn’t need special casing beyond checking the binding + expiry.
- Dual-read migration: in shadow mode compare v1 vs v2 decisions and emit metric on mismatch (don’t change behavior yet).


Appendix A: Example route -> permission mapping snippet
Gateway route table entry (pseudo):
- method: POST
  path: /v1/orgs/{org_id}/routing-policies/{policy_id}:update
  action: controlplane.routingPolicies.update
  scope_from_request:
    org_id: path.org_id
    project_id: body.project_id (if present)
    env_id: body.env_id (if present)
  resource:
    type: routing_policy
    id: path.policy_id

Concern: body parsing in gateway. Prefer moving project_id/env_id into path for v2 endpoints.


Appendix B: Minimal “authz decision context” to propagate
When gateway allows, attach internal metadata so services can:
- correlate decisions
- optionally skip re-evaluation only if request is internal and signed (but we probably won’t skip; still useful for debugging)

Proposed internal header (signed or via internal mTLS trust boundary):
- X-Redwood-Authz-Context: base64(json({subject_id, action, scope, policy_version, gateway_decision_id}))

We should be careful: don’t treat this as proof of authorization unless we add cryptographic signing + strict validation.


End
